script.title: Price Elasticity of Demand explained simply
script.caption_hook: Petrol gets costlier, yet we still buy it. Why?

lines.say: Ma'am, petrol gets costlier, but people still buy it. Why?
That's price elasticity of demand. It shows how fast buyers react when price changes.
So how do we measure that reaction?
Elasticity equals percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. Percent over percent.
Can you show a number example?
Sure. Samosa price rises 10%, demand falls 20%. Twenty divided by ten gives two. We ignore the negative sign.
Two... is that big or small?
Compare it with one. Above one is elastic: buyers escape. Below one is inelastic: buyers stay, like with petrol.
Oh! And what happens to the seller's revenue?
When price rises, elastic demand cuts revenue. Inelastic demand raises it. Unitary keeps it the same.
So our samosa, with Ed two, loses revenue?
Exactly! Price up, quantity falls proportionately more, so revenue falls.
Remember: percent over percent, then compare with one.

check_notes: Writer: Samosa example: price ₹10 to ₹11 (10%), quantity 100 to 80 (20%), revenue ₹1,000 to ₹880, falls. Ed shown as absolute value 2, with a note on the negative sign. Petrol described as inelastic, a tendency for necessities.

Checker: Line 2 voice and board sub ('how fast buyers react'): elasticity measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price (the degree of responsiveness), not how fast. Speed is a separate idea, since time period is one of the determinants of elasticity. Correct version: 'It shows how much buyers react when price changes' / sub = 'degree of responsiveness'.

Checker: Line 13 board ('%Q over %P'): the Δ is missing. It should read '%ΔQ over %ΔP' (percentage change in quantity demanded over percentage change in price), to match the formula on the Line 4 board.
